title: The talbiyah
hookLine: here I am, O Allah, here I am, no partner have You

cards: Somebody calls your name across a room. Before you've decided anything, before you know what they want, you answer. Here.
Yes? I'm here. In the Qur'an, Ibrahim is told to make a call of his own.

Pickthall's translation of surah twenty-two: "And proclaim unto mankind the Pilgrimage. They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine." A call goes out.
On the roads to Mecca, people answer it, out loud, over and over. Today, the answer.

teach.h: HERE I AM, O ALLAH, HERE I AM.
teach.b: First, the words. Abdullah ibn Umar reported the talbiyah of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and it's kept in Sahih al-Bukhari. In Arabic it begins: labbayk Allahumma labbayk.
In English, roughly: here I am, O Allah, here I am. Here I am, You have no partner, here I am. Praise and blessing are Yours, and the dominion.
You have no partner. That's all of it, a handful of short lines said again and again. You first heard labbayk back on day two hundred eighty-four.
Second, the shape of the word.
Labbayk isn't a request. It's a reply, the word for answering someone who has called you: here I am, at your service. The pilgrim isn't starting a conversation, but responding to one.
Some readers connect that to Ibrahim's call in surah twenty-two: he proclaimed, and pilgrims, generation after generation, are still answering.
Third, the line that comes twice: no partner have You. In a journey full of crowds, rituals and holy places, the talbiyah keeps pointing past all of it, to one God alone. Fourth, the sound.
A report in Tirmidhi has the Prophet saying that the angel Jibril came and told him to have his companions raise their voices with the talbiyah.
So the roads, the buses, the airports and the tents carry it out loud, men's voices raised, women's usually lower. A pilgrim begins it on entering ihram and keeps it going for days.
The man in yesterday's story, who died in ihram, would be raised still saying it. Here I am.

how: Pilgrims begin reciting the talbiyah when they enter ihram and repeat it often, men aloud and women more quietly, through the days of the pilgrimage until the stoning on the day of sacrifice, according to the reports of the Prophet's Hajj.

o: the call to prayer sung from a mosque tower
the pilgrim's reply to God's call: here I am
a request for forgiveness said at the Ka'ba

s: labbayk is a request for help
it's a reply: here I am, answering a call.
in Pickthall's Qur'an, Ibrahim is told to proclaim the pilgrimage
the talbiyah is said once, at the Ka'ba
pilgrims begin it at ihram and repeat it, out loud, for days.

games.q: you've just entered ihram and your bus pulls onto the road to Mecca. what does the Prophet's practice suggest you do?
o: stay silent until you reach the Ka'ba.
raise your voice with the talbiyah.
games.why: a report in Tirmidhi says Jibril told the Prophet to have his companions raise their voices with the talbiyah.

practice: If you're Muslim, or pray, say labbayk Allahumma labbayk quietly and slowly a few times, and notice that each line is an answer.
If not, let the English run through your mind, here I am, and notice what it would mean to answer a call before you know everything it will ask.

wordCard.voice: Talbiyah. The pilgrim's cry, labbayk, here I am, said from the moment of ihram. Today's word.

orig.note: here I am, at your service: the answer to a call, and the first word of the talbiyah.

carryVoice: Your line: labbayk. Here I am: an answer, given before the question is even finished. Until tomorrow.
